body:
**Michael Bayer ([@zzzeek](https://github.com/zzzeek)) wrote:**

at this point i think the entire Unicode type is ready to go.  it was imitated from SQLObject but we are very different from that now.  String already does unicode conversion so we've been violating DRY for over a year....all it needs is an extra flag.   also, MSSQL can have its NTEXT or whatever but i dont want to add that to types, and i definitely dont want to start putting in `__new__()` tricks...i want the architecture to work.  since i cant easily test ms-sql i never knew this issue existed so i will look into it.

**paj ([@paj](https://github.com/paj)) wrote:**

Yeah, that's one approach. Most databases only have a single string type, with a database option to say if that type supports unicode. MSSQL is different; it has VARCHAR for 8-bit strings and NVARCHAR for unicode. Still, I think having a single SA string type will work - it will become NVARCHAR on MSSQL. Anyone who really needs VARCHAR (rare I expect) can still use the MSVarchar SA type.

On __new__() tricks, there is an existing String.__new__ which detects zero-length and returns a TEXT() instead. I would prefer different behaviour personally, especially as a number of databases support VARCHAR without a length specified (both Postgres and MSSQL 2005).

BTW, if you want to use MSSQL, you can download SQL Server Express 2005 for free.

**Michael Bayer ([@zzzeek](https://github.com/zzzeek)) wrote:**

ok the *real* reason that `Unicode` really has to not be a `TypeDecorator` and things need to get flattened into `String` is because of `ADOMSNVarchar` - where it seems apparent that when using an `NVarchar` with ADO, you specifically *dont* want unicode conversion to happen.  so right there, the "unicode being a decorator" paradigm blows up, since the unicode convert/no convert decision is very specifically part of a databases implementation of a type.

so this patch addresses the errant `__new__()` method in there, provides a way engine-specific subclasses could replace String's `TEXT` conversion with a no-length `VARCHAR` if they wanted (by overriding `get_search_list()`), converts `Unicode` to a `String` using a very quick metaclass (which Im not even sure if we need at this point) and also removes the `MSUnicode` types in favor of a simpler mapping of `Unicode->MSNVarchar/ADOMSNVarchar`.

I really would turn on my windows box and try it tonight but I have to run out for a bit, so if it works on your end we can commit.

same patch sans metaclass

(original author: ram) Right, pymssql doesn't support unicode.

**Michael Bayer ([@zzzeek](https://github.com/zzzeek)) wrote:**

doesnt support unicode meaning, we cant even send in a utf-8 encoded bytestring ?  you would think that would be an easy fix on the pymssql side of things....

**paj ([@paj](https://github.com/paj)) wrote:**

Yes, the patch works fine on MSSQL. I like it, especially as it clears up the internals.

I though pymssql was utf-8 encoding unicode, so that it works from the SA point of view, although if a different read the database it would not necessarily understand it. Also, the SQL length() function will return the wrong values.

**Anonymous wrote:**

(original author: ram) no I meant doesn't support unicode as in doesn't support MS-SQL unicode-specific (UTF-16) columns.

normal string types (for MSSQL, that's CHAR(), VARCHAR() and TEXT), all are 8-bit strings, and work fine with utf-8 for any of the MSSQL modules, including pymssql.

the length() function will only return the wrong value if there are non-ascii characters stored.

**Michael Bayer ([@zzzeek](https://github.com/zzzeek)) wrote:**

do we want to make any changes to the `Unicode` type as represented with pymssql ?  since `Unicode` seems to be essentially useless when using pymssql.

at this point, all of the string types take a convert_unicode argument.  so if you wanted utf-8 conversion with pymssql, youd say `CHAR(convert_unicode=True)`, `VARCHAR(convert_unicode=True)`, etc.

so...this ticket can be closed ?

**Anonymous wrote:**

(original author: ram) I think I may be the last person still using pymssql; and this works for me, so yeah, good to go.
